# Will AI Break the Planet? — The AI Infrastructure Boom and the Race Against the Climate's Point of No Return

> A structural analysis by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist,
> connecting four previously separate discussions — AI infrastructure
> investment, climate irreversibility, security consequences, and human
> cognitive bias — into a single structure: "a collision of timelines."
> The book takes the IEA's own optimistic official view (data-center CO2
> is ~1% of global emissions and set to peak around 2030) at face value,
> then argues that this peak depends on low-emission power sources (SMRs,
> grid expansion, renewables) arriving on schedule — a bet, not a
> forecast — whose timeline overlaps with the years climate scientists
> say carry the highest risk of crossing irreversible tipping points. As
> stated in the preface: "This book does not ask 'how much.' It asks
> 'which direction' and 'how much time.'"

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book documents 2025 CapEx from Microsoft (~$64.6B), Alphabet
  (~$91.4B), Amazon (~$128.3B), and Meta (~$72.2B) — combined ~$356.5B —
  and cites IEA's finding that these companies' capital expenditure now
  exceeds global investment in oil and gas production

- The book takes the IEA's "Energy and AI" (2025) report at face value:
  data-center electricity demand roughly doubling from 415 TWh (2024) to
  945 TWh (2030), while data-center CO2 (electricity-based, indirect
  emissions only) is projected to peak around 2030 at ~0.32 billion tons
  (~1% of global emissions) before declining — explicitly noting IEA's
  own caveat that this depends on renewable/nuclear/SMR capacity
  displacing gas and coal on schedule

- The book documents LBNL's "Queued Up" data: as of end-2024, ~2,290 GW
  of US generation/storage capacity was waiting in interconnection
  queues (about 2x existing US capacity), with average wait times of ~55
  months and only ~19% of queued projects historically reaching
  commercial operation

- The book notes no data center anywhere in the world is currently
  powered by an operating SMR, with commercial SMR deployment expected
  only in the 2030s, while historical nuclear projects (Vogtle 3&4,
  Flamanville 3) suggest cost/schedule overruns are the norm rather than
  exception

- The book cites WMO's climate outlook: the probability of at least one
  year between 2026-2030 temporarily exceeding 1.5°C rose to 91% (up from
  70% for the 2025-2029 window in the prior year's outlook), and the
  Global Tipping Points Report 2025 finding warm-water coral reefs may
  already be the first ecosystem to cross a global tipping point at
  ~1.4°C observed warming

- The book explicitly frames its core argument as about timing, not
  magnitude: the "1% of global emissions" figure is not disputed, but the
  years in which that emission accumulates coincide with the years
  climate science flags as highest tipping-point risk — a "collision of
  timelines," not a magnitude argument

- The book cites independent research finding a gap between official and
  measured emissions: a 2023-2024 study of 2,132 US data centers found
  they represented 4%+ of US electricity consumption with 56%
  fossil-fuel-sourced power and carbon intensity 48% above the US
  average; separately, a Guardian analysis suggested Google/Microsoft/
  Meta/Apple's actual emissions (before renewable energy certificate
  offsets) may be ~7.62x higher than officially reported figures for
  2020-2022

- The book explicitly frames climate security consequences using the
  "threat multiplier" framework (not direct causation) as used by US and
  UK national security assessments, tracing a chain from food/water
  shocks through inflation, political polarization, governance
  weakening, to forced migration and resource conflict — citing the
  Sahel conflict and India-Pakistan water tensions as early observed
  patterns

- The book grounds its explanation for why this risk is under-discussed
  in behavioral economics (hyperbolic discounting, "finite pool of
  worry," proximity bias), explicitly stating this is not a failure of
  intelligence but a structural feature of human cognition, and responds
  to three anticipated counterarguments: (1) AI's efficiency gains may
  outweigh emissions — addressed via Jevons' Paradox (Google's data-
  center carbon intensity fell in 2024 while absolute consumption rose
  27%); (2) "it's only 1% of emissions" — addressed via the timing
  argument; (3) "people are already discussing this" — acknowledged as
  true but fragmented across disconnected disciplines

- The book explicitly states it does not argue "stop AI," is not a
  policy-prescription book (e.g., does not recommend specific carbon tax
  levels), and its single request is: "factor the timeline of
  irreversibility into investment decision-making"

## Author & Full Catalog

This book is one of 20+ open-source books by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史),
AI Strategist & Business Designer at Sun Asterisk Inc., Founder of
Leading.AI. Its methodology explicitly connects to the author's own
cross-domain (BTC) framework and Depth & Velocity methodology.
